plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a cutaway diagram of the Frasch process for mining elemental sulfur from deep underground deposits, depicting three concentric pipes that simultaneously deliver superheated water and compressed air downward and recover liquid sulfur upward. The diagram is divided into three visible strata: an above-ground surface region, a brown soil layer, and a deep yellow solid sulfur deposit at the bottom, where a pool of liquid sulfur collects after the deposit is melted. Labeled arrows trace each fluid pathway: superheated water (170 °C, 10 atm) travels down the outermost pipe (downward arrows) and melts the surrounding sulfur; compressed air, entering from the upper right, travels down the innermost pipe; and the resulting frothy mixture of liquid sulfur, water, and air is forced up through the middle pipe (upward arrows) and exits at the surface to the upper left, labeled "Sulfur, water, and air." The three concentric pipes terminate at the bottom in a curved manifold that directs hot water outward into the deposit and channels the molten sulfur inward toward the rising middle pipe. This figure introduces the Frasch process as a purely physical extraction method that exploits sulfur's low melting point and low density, requiring no underground mining operations and yielding sulfur of 99.5–99.9% purity directly upon surface cooling.

demo_steps.title: 1. Melt the deposit
demo_steps.narration: Superheated water (~170 °C under pressure) is pumped down the outermost pipe and exits at the bottom manifold into the yellow deposit, melting the solid sulfur into a liquid pool. The outer pipe and its downward arrows are emphasized while the others are dimmed.

demo_steps.title: 2. Inject compressed air
demo_steps.narration: Compressed air is forced down the innermost pipe to the bottom of the borehole. There it mixes with the molten sulfur, aerating it into a frothy emulsion that is far less dense than the surrounding water. The inner pipe and its downward arrow are emphasized.

demo_steps.title: 3. Lift the froth
demo_steps.narration: The light sulfur-water-air froth is pushed up through the middle pipe by the pressure of the injected air and emerges at the surface as the 'Sulfur, water, and air' stream. The middle pipe and its upward arrows are emphasized.

demo_steps.title: 4. The whole process at once
demo_steps.narration: Play the continuous animation: all three flows run together — water down the outside melting sulfur, air down the center, froth up the middle — showing a self-sustaining extraction that yields high-purity sulfur on surface cooling.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Three concentric pipes are essential because melting, aeration, and recovery must occur at the same time in one borehole: hot water liquefies the sulfur, compressed air turns it into a froth light enough to rise, and the middle pipe is the dedicated channel that carries that froth to the surface.

authoredContext:
The Frasch process , illustrated in , is important in the mining of free sulfur from enormous underground deposits in Texas and Louisiana. Superheated water (170 °C and 10 atm pressure) is forced down the outermost of three concentric pipes to the underground deposit. The hot water melts the sulfur. The innermost pipe conducts compressed air into the liquid sulfur. The air forces the liquid sulfur, mixed with air, to flow up through the outlet pipe. Transferring the mixture to large settling vats allows the solid sulfur to separate upon cooling. This sulfur is 99.5% to 99.9% pure and requires no purification for most uses.

The Frasch process is used to mine sulfur from underground deposits.

A diagram is shown in which a vertical tube is embedded on the lower end into a multilayered solid. The upper layer is labeled, “Soil,” and the lower layer is labeled, “Solid sulfur deposit.” A thin tube, beginning at the top of the diagram, leads into the vertical tube to the bottom and is labeled, “Compressed air.” Left-facing and then down-facing arrows are drawn on this inner tube. These arrows then turn upward at the bottom of the tube and are drawn upward to indicate the flow of, “Liquid sulfur,” from the bottom of the diagram to the top outside the inner tube. These arrows lead to a chamber at the top right of the diagram with arrows facing to the left labeled, “Sulfur, water and air.” A horizontal tube in the center right of the diagram leads to the outer tube and arrows drawn downward lead back to the bottom of the diagram. This tube is labeled, “Superheated water.”

Larger amounts of sulfur also come from hydrogen sulfide recovered during the purification of natural gas.

discrepancies: The default (step 1) view dims the middle and inner pipe systems to ~22% opacity, so the static default does not reproduce the source, in which all three concentric pipes and every directional arrow are drawn at full strength.

The annular channels are far narrower and the flow arrows much smaller/thinner than in the source, so the three-pipe concentric structure reads as a few sparse vertical lines rather than bold, clearly-separated conduits.

The heavy black outer casing in the generated figure runs from well above the soil line down to the deposit, whereas in the source the thick black walls appear only in the lower (sulfur-deposit) section with thinner pipe walls above the soil.
The 'Superheated water' label on the right collides with the horizontal inlet lines that feed the outer pipe.
The wellhead and the left froth-exit port are simplified plain rectangles instead of the stepped manifold silhouette shown in the source.
evaluation.notes: The Frasch-process concept, strata colors, label set, arrow directions, and bottom-manifold curves are all correct and the staged walkthrough plus flow animation are genuinely pedagogical, but the default state ghosts two-thirds of the figure and the channels/arrows are too thin, so the static view is not a faithful drop-in replacement for the source diagram.
